episode_title: Competition and Foreign Investment Law for a Resilient Canada: Recapping the 2026 CBA Fall Conference

real_qa.q: What were the two competing approaches to competition policy debated at the 2026 CBA Fall Conference on resilient Canada?
real_qa.r: One camp believes Canada needs to invest in Canadian champions to compete globally at scale. The other camp argues the focus should remain on the domestic economy and whether concentration is good for Canadians. Kate McNeese noted both sides have merit: efficiencies and scale matter, but concentration is still concentration and people need to afford to live in Canada.
real_qa.requete: 2026 CBA Fall Conference national champions debate

real_qa.q: Did the Competition Act efficiency defense, removed in amendments from 2022-2024, see renewed support at the October 2026 conference?
real_qa.r: Yes. Kate McNeese noted that one of the surprises at the conference was the amount of support for the efficiency defense, 10 years after it was removed. However, she expressed skepticism about reinserting it, calling it a potential squandering of legislative firepower given the effort taken to remove it two years prior.

real_qa.q: What new Investment Canada Act filing requirement is coming in Q1 2027 related to national security?
real_qa.r: A mandatory national security notification regime will come online in approximately Q1 2027. It sets out a large range of sectors that will be subject to mandatory pre-closing filing requirements, expanding the scope of national security analysis beyond traditional defense and sensitive infrastructure to include supply chain, critical minerals, and emerging technologies.
real_qa.requete: Investment Canada Act mandatory national security notification Q1 2027

real_qa.q: Why might sector-specific competition rules in Canada create practical challenges despite their appeal?
real_qa.r: Kate McNeese explained that sector-specific rules face a temporal problem: sectors that matter today may not matter in four years, creating a scenario where government would need separate competition regimes for every industry that becomes politically important. She also noted that Canada's existing Competition Act is flexible enough to address market-specific concerns through product and geographic market analysis.

real_qa.q: What predictability concerns did panelists raise about the Investment Canada Act net benefit review process?
real_qa.r: Panelists Anita Banshevik and Martha Hall Finlay emphasized the need for consistency and predictability in merger reviews. Kate McNeese highlighted that unpredictable timelines and potentially infinite extensions of the statutory period create challenges. She advocated for more guidance on appropriate undertakings and comparable pricing certainty, arguing predictability could reduce the chilling effect on investment.
real_qa.requete: Investment Canada Act net benefit review predictability undertakings

guest.bio_context: Kate McNeese is a frequent podcast contributor and one of the 2026 CBA Fall Conference co-chairs alongside Shuley Rodell. She is a competition lawyer with expertise in merger review, foreign investment law, and policy analysis of Canadian economic regulation.
